$$\sum_{v}\binom{d(v)}{2}\ge 2\binom{n}{2}=n(n-1),$$
and the condition forces $\delta\ge 3$ (a degree-3 vertex forces its neighborhood to be a triangle; a degree-2 vertex could not supply two common neighbors with one of its own neighbors).

To minimize $m=\frac12\sum d(v)$ under these constraints, convexity of $\binom{d}{2}$ dictates pushing degrees to the extremes. The extremal construction takes two universal vertices $a,b$ (adjacent to everything, including each other) and a minimum-size graph $H$ on the remaining $n-2$ vertices with $\delta(H)\ge 1$ (a near-perfect matching). This yields
$$S(n)=2(n-2)+1+\left\lceil\frac{n-2}{2}\right\rceil=2n-4+\left\lceil\frac n2\right\rceil=\left\lceil\frac{5n-8}{2}\right\rceil.$$

Checking optimality via the counting bound: for $n=2k$ and $m=5k-5$, the maximum possible $\sum\binom{d}{2}$ (attained at degrees $2k-1,2k-3,3,\dots,3$) is $4k^2-4k+1<4k^2-2k$. For $n=2k+1$ and $m=5k-2$, the maximum (at $2k,2k-1,3,\dots,3$) is $4k^2+2k-2<4k^2+2k$. Hence no smaller $m$ works, and the construction is exact.
